text: To understand the phenomenon of the experimental data, the temperature distribution of PT from CFD data is depicted in Figure 19. The axial temperature gradient inside the PT is not uniformly distributed, while a relatively significant temperature gradient can be observed near the wall surface. Radial temperatures are significantly different at different angles, consistent with the experimental results. In addition, the highest temperature is found close to the hot-end PT. This is in agreement with the trend of the experimentally measured temperatures. The complex flow of helium inside the PT results in the mixing of hot and cold helium. This is the reason for the nonuniform distribution of temperature.

7.5. Flow characteristics of the main components

To reveal the cause of the non-uniform temperature gradient within the PT, the helium flow characteristics in the PT are investigated through CFD data. The results find that there are four flow types in the PT, as shown in Figure 20. The gas parcels inside the PT are classified into three kinds. The red gas parcel moves at the hot end, and the blue one moves at the cold end. Additionally, the yellow one is constantly considered a gas piston. The flow styles Ⅰ and Ⅱ are the common flow types. The flow style Ⅰ corresponds to the expansion process, while the flow style Ⅱ corresponds to the compressor process. At an instant of one cycle, the flow styles Ⅲ and Ⅳ are observed in PT.

image_caption: Figure. 20 Four flow types in the PT.

text: The velocity contours and streamlines for the PT at a cycle are displayed in Figure 21. The process of forming the flow pattern Ⅳ is described in Figure 21(a)-(c). For Figure 21(a), there are two gas parcels at the cold end, resulting in the development of two vortices and a zero velocity interface. It is demonstrated that the velocity amplitude of the helium at the position of PT is zero. The vortices gradually expand in the radial direction from the wall to the axial in the radial direction and grow at 0.41 T, leading to the formation of pattern Ⅳ. While the vortices gradually become smaller at 0.44 T. The process of forming the flow pattern Ⅲ is depicted in Figure 21(d)-(f). For Figure 21(d), the collision is observed at both ends of PT with gas particles entering. This will lead to the formation of miniature vortices at the wall of the cold end. From Figure 21(d) to Figure 21(e), it can be found that the zero-velocity interface moves from the cold end to the hot end, owing to the oscillating flow in the PT during the process. The vortices are generated at the mid-axial of the hot end. The zero-velocity interface enhances the expansion process. Therefore, the vortices are formed in the cold of PT, increasing the energy loss. In addition, the complex helium flow in the PT results

text: To investigate the effect of working frequency on the flow pattern in the pulse tube, the flow styles Ⅲ and Ⅳ for the PT are shown in Figure 22 when the working frequency is 69 Hz. It can be noticed that the number and size of vortices are comparable at the working frequencies of 64 and 69 Hz. The zero-velocity interface appears later when the working frequency is 69 Hz. Moreover, the scale of the zero-velocity interface in PT is smaller at the working frequency of 69 Hz.

The FSs are equipped at both ends of the PT. Which are considered porous zones in Fluent, utilized to prevent the formation of vortices. However, the FSs of APRPTHP cannot completely prevent the formation of vortices. The St number is adopted to explain flow style Ⅲ and Ⅳ. The St number is calculated by equation (30).

where � is the working frequency, � is the characteristic diameter, � is the velocity of the working fluid. The St number varies with working frequency and velocity when the diameter is constant. The velocity increases with the increase in working frequency. It can be found that the influence of velocity on the St number is more significant than frequency. Therefore, the formation, evolution, and shedding of vortices can be controlled by an appropriate St number.

text: Due to the oscillating flow of the helium in the APRPTHP, the helium flow style at the Tjunction zone is not identical to its flow style at the other components. Six flow styles are discovered at the T-junction structure in a cycle, as shown in Figure 23. The numbers and scales of vortices are periodically generated when helium flows through the T-junction structure. From 1/16T to 4/16T, the vortices at the acoustic power recovery tube are gradually developed and then fade away. From 5/16T to 7/16T, the vortices are produced on one side of the T-junction and become magnified. From 8/16T to 10/16T, small-scale vortices are generated at the wall and then disappear. From 11/16T to 15/16T, the vortices are generated at both places at the same time. The scale of the vortices is gradually grown, then merges into one to fill the entire tube. This situation leads to significant flow loss. Finally, the vortices disappear at the 16/16T. This phenomenon is the result of the various processes of vortices conducted by the contraction and expansion of the helium, flow detachment, velocity collisions of the helium, and cyclical variation of the flow direction. The periodic variation in flow direction is the most significant factor that leads to the change process of vortices. Therefore, a large energy loss is generated at the T-junction.

text: To clearly estimate the energy loss from the T-junction, the PV power loss is calculated quantitatively by equation (16). The acoustic power is recovered at the ES and transported to the ACS. Subsequently, the recovered acoustic power is transported to the heat pump part at the Tjunction. Therefore, the sum of PV power at the heat pump inlet and PV power loss at the T-junction equals the sum of PV in CS and the ACS.

where $W _ { P V I }$ is the PV power in the compressor chamber, $W _ { P V 2 }$ is the PV power in the ACS, and $W _ { P V 3 }$ is the PV power at the heat pump inlet. The PV power loss is 12.9 W at the T-junction when the heating capacity is 251.4 W at 353 K. The PV power loss is about 12.9% of the PV power in CS. The performance of APRPTHP can be improved by optimizing the T-junction structure.

8. Conclusions

An efficient high heating-capacity APRPTHP working at 353 K is designed, manufactured, and studied. The impacts of hot-end temperature, cold-end temperature, and working frequency on the performance of APRPTHP are evaluated by experiment. Based on the validated threedimensional simulation, the temperature distribution and flow characteristics inside the APRPTHP are revealed. The following conclusions are drawn.

(1) The optimal working of APRPTHP is 64 Hz in the experiment. The performance of APRPTHP is improved by decreasing the working temperature. When the input electric power and working temperature are 175 W and 353 K, APRPTHP can obtain a heating capacity of 226 W, and its relative Carnot efficiency is 36.5%. The phase difference between the displacer and piston of 81.25° is measured. It is dependent on working frequency, while it is not affected by other operating conditions.

(2) The helium flow direction varies complexly at one cycle, resulting in the generation of the vortices and zero-velocity interface. When the working frequency increases, the zero-velocity interface is observed later, and the vortices are smaller. As a result, the temperature distribution inside PT is non-uniform. While the temperature distribution for the REG is a linear gradient owing to the presence of the stack wire mesh. Finally, the phase difference for mass flow and pressure wave of 0° is observed inside the PT.

(3) The helium from three directions is gathered, leading to complex variations of the flow direction. The acoustic power loss is 13.7 W when the heating capacity is 251.4 W at 353 K. The acoustic power loss is about 12.9% of the input acoustic power.
